Abstract.

A thorough analysis is performed to find traveling waves in a qualitative reaction-diffusion system inspired by a predator-prey model. We provide rigorous results coming from a standard local stability analysis, numerical bifurcation analysis, and relevant computations of invariant manifolds to exhibit homoclinic and heteroclinic connections, and periodic orbits in the associated traveling wave system with four components. In so doing, we present and describe a zoo of different traveling wave solutions. In addition, homoclinic chaos is manifested via both saddle-focus and focus-focus bifurcations as well as a Belyakov point. An actual computation of global invariant manifolds near a focus-focus homoclinic bifurcation is also presented to unravel a multiplicity of wave solutions in the model.

Key words and phrases: 
Homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits, traveling waves, invariant manifolds, bifurcation analysis.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
37N25, 35C07, 92D40, 37C29, 37D10, 37G20, 35Q92

1. Introduction

Invariant manifold analysis and global bifurcations are among the avant garde of research topics in nonlinear dynamical systems. From the seminal works of L. P. Shilnikov [1, 48, 49] onwards, global bifurcations and invariant manifolds have gained a lot of attention from the dynamical systems community; see, for instance, the survey by Guckenheimer et al. [20], and references therein for different high-profile scenarios including slow-fast dynamics, homoclinic orbits in high-dimensions, and traveling waves phenomena. Geometrically, global bifurcations of vector fields are associated with invariant manifolds of equilibria and/or periodic orbits, quasiperiodic invariant tori [21, 23, 30], and slow manifolds of systems with multiple timescales [36, 37]. Perturbations of the system parameters typically cause global rearrangements of such invariant manifolds, leading to reorganizations of the overall dynamics in the phase space. These can bring forth the creation/destruction of homoclinic and heteroclinic connections, and the (dis)appeareance of attracting (repelling) invariant objects, including periodic orbits and even chaotic dynamics [30, 50]. Hence, global invariant manifolds emerge as the “building blocks” of a dynamical system, i.e., those essential objects help to explain how the overall “architecture” of phase space is organized.

One of the applications of invariant manifold analysis lies on the existence of traveling wave solutions for reaction-diffusion equations. This kind of solution emerges as a suitable mathematical approach to describe wave-like spatial movement of populations, transport of nutrients and biological substances, etc.; see, for instance, the textbooks [39, 38] and references therein. Indeed, traveling waves represent spatiotemporal transitions from one homogeneous steady state to another one, or to itself [23, 32, 38, 46, 53]. Typically, the mathematical analysis to find this kind of solution involves the reduction of the reaction-diffusion equations into a system of ordinary differential equations in which one searches for heteroclinic or homoclinic orbits. However, the problem of obtaining these connecting orbits and associated global (un)stable manifolds is a challenging task. With the exception of a few concrete examples (see, e.g., [23]), in general, there are no analytical expressions for homoclinic orbits or non-local normal forms. Hence, it is frequent to make use of reductions to Poincaré maps in suitable cross sections, center manifold reductions and other analytical approaches to prove the existence of intersecting invariant manifolds giving rise to homoclinic and heteroclinic connections; see [15, 24, 25, 35, 43, 51, 54] for different examples.

The purpose of this paper is to establish the existence of traveling wave solutions for the following reaction-diffusion system:

{ut=D1​ux​x+u⁡(u−m)​(1−u)​(u+v)−α​u​v,vt=D2​vx​x+β​u​v−γ​v​(u+v),\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{t}=D_{1}u_{xx}+u(u-m)(1-u)(u+v)-\alpha uv\,,\\[6.45831pt] v_{t}=D_{2}v_{xx}+\beta uv-\gamma v(u+v)\,,\end{array}\right.

where short notation is used for partial derivatives: wt=∂w/∂tw_{t}=\partial w/\partial t and wx​x=∂2w/∂x2w_{xx}=\partial^{2}w/\partial x^{2}. In (1), u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) are the unknown variables as functions of the spatial variable x∈[−L,L]x\in[-L,L] and time t>0t>0. The characteristic length of the state variables interaction domain is assumed to be such that L→∞L\to\infty as traveling waves solutions are known to arise in systems as (1) (see e.g. [9, 25, 31, 34]); diffusion rates D1,D2>0D_{1},D_{2}>0 correspond to mobilities which are a measure of the spatial dispersion efficiency of uu and vv, respectively [38].

System (1) is inspired by a predator-prey model from [5] accounting for strong Allee effect on prey and ratio-dependent functional response. However, the main purpose of (1) is not to duplicate exactly quantitative aspects of the predator-prey interactions from the model it is inspired by. Rather, (1) is meant as an elementary, minimal model in which one can display the sorts of mathematical relations between variables underlying the connections in [5]. Hence, we refrain from calling uu and vv as the prey and predators, respectively, in order to avoid misunderstandings with the interpretation of results of the conceptual model (1). We note that our approach to (1) is similar to that of other qualitative models in biology such as the celebrated FitzHugh-Nagumo model for action potentials in neurons [38], or the Izhikevich [26], Hindmarsh-Rose [47] and the canonical Ermentrout-Kopell [17] models. Indeed, while these abstract models are constructed less closely to physiological features and thus less interpretable, they succeed in portray diverse essential neuronal behaviors with just the minimal mathematical ingredients (see [16] and references therein).

With a strategic combination of numerical methods for invariant manifolds and bifurcation theory, we find the traveling wave solutions identifying each of them as a specific heteroclinic/homoclinic connection or a periodic orbit in the four-dimensional phase space of the associated ODEs. We classify these solutions into 12 different classes depending on the topological type of the associated orbit. We also determine conditions on the model parameters so that there is such a particular kind of solution and identify homoclinic chaotic dynamics as one of the sources of complicated behavior.

Today, homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits can readily be computed and continued with software packages like Auto [14] (with its extension HomCont [10]) and Matcont [12] with high accuracy. In addition, one can locate homoclinic and heteroclinic connections as intersections of global invariant manifolds. This can be achieved by direct computation and inspection of the manifolds [3, 6], or by setting additional techniques such as Lin’s method [27]. While one-dimensional invariant manifolds can be approximated using straightforward integration from a given initial condition, the computation of higher-dimensional manifolds of equilibria and periodic orbits requires advanced numerical techniques. The two-dimensional global manifolds in this paper are computed as families of orbit segments, which can be obtained as solutions of a suitable boundary value problem (BVP), irrespective of the vector field undergoing a homoclinic or heteroclinic bifurcation. This allows us to make use of Auto to implement and solve the BVP; then, the manifold is “built up” by continuation of the respective orbit segments [28, 29]; see also [4, 2, 6, 20] for further details and applications. Moreover, while some works have dealt with traveling waves associated with three-dimensional vector fields [33, 51, 54], our problem involves a four-dimensional phase space, which is a major challenge. Although the human brain is efficient when capturing depth in flat images of 3-dimensional objects, this ability is not as effective in higher dimensions [11, 40]. When trying to visualize objects in a 4D phase space —such as invariant manifolds—, standard projections may give rise to false intersections between them. These artifacts due to projections must be detected and differentiated from real intersections to ensure or discard the existence of homoclinic or heteroclinic connections. To do so, we make extensive use of dynamical systems theory and topological arguments to justify our findings. In addition, wave trains are found as periodic orbits originating via Hopf bifurcations; see also [15, 24, 25, 35, 42] for other uses of this theoretical argument.

This paper is organized as follows: §2 presents some definitions, notation and preliminary results. Local stability analysis of steady states is included in §3, while a bifurcation analysis is presented in §4. Wave pulses, wave trains and wave fronts are discussed in §5, §6 and §7, respectively. §8 presents a description of the multiple wave fronts found near a focus-focus homoclinic bifurcation. §9 discusses the influence of the propagation speed and the diffusion ratio on the occurrence of the different wave pulses. §10 analyzes the existence of traveling fronts in two invariant planes. Finally, §11 presents a summary and discussion of the main results.

2. Preliminaries and first examples

For future convenience, the first step to study traveling wave solutions in (1) is to make a time rescaling and a change of parameters given, respectively, by

t→D2​t,(d,s,b,g,a,m)=(D1D2,1D2,s​β,s​γ,s​α,m)∈ℝ+5×]0,1[.t\to D_{2}t,\qquad(d,s,b,g,a,m)=\left(\dfrac{D_{1}}{D_{2}},\dfrac{1}{D_{2}},s\beta,s\gamma,s\alpha,m\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{5}_{+}\times]0,1[.

Thus, we can write system (1) equivalently as

{ut=d​ux​x+s​u​(u−m)​(1−u)​(u+v)−a​u​v;vt=vx​x+b​u​v−g​v​(u+v).\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{t}=du_{xx}+su(u-m)(1-u)(u+v)-auv;\\[6.45831pt] v_{t}=v_{xx}+buv-gv(u+v).\end{array}\right.

Here, d=D1/D2d=D_{1}/D_{2} represents the ratio of diffusion rates of uu and vv, respectively, and appears as an explicit parameter in (2). If d>1d>1 (resp. d<1d<1), uu is more (resp. less) efficient to disperse in space compared to vv.

We now consider the so-called wave variable z=x+c​tz=x+ct, where c>0c>0 is the wave speed, and we look for solutions of (2) of the form U⁡(z)=u⁡(x,t)U(z)=u(x,t), V⁡(z)=v⁡(x,t)V(z)=v(x,t). Applying the chain rule and substituting this into (2), we obtain the following set of second order ordinary differential equations

{c​d​Ud​z=d​d2​Ud​z2+s​U​(U−m)​(1−U)​(U+V)−a​U​V;c​d​Vd​z=d2​Vd​z2+b​U​V−g​V​(U+V).\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}c\dfrac{dU}{dz}=d\dfrac{d^{2}U}{dz^{2}}+sU(U-m)(1-U)(U+V)-aUV;\\[6.45831pt] c\dfrac{dV}{dz}=\dfrac{d^{2}V}{dz^{2}}+bUV-gV(U+V).\end{array}\right.

Naming the auxiliary variables W=d​U/d​zW=dU/dz and R=d​V/d​zR=dV/dz, system (2) can be expressed equivalently as the vector field

X:{d​Ud​z=W,d​Vd​z=R,d​Wd​z=1d​(c​W−s​U​(U−m)​(1−U)​(U+V)+a​U​V),d​Rd​z=c​R−b​U​V+g​V​(U+V).\displaystyle X:\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\dfrac{dU}{dz}=W,\\[6.45831pt] \dfrac{dV}{dz}=R,\\[6.45831pt] \dfrac{dW}{dz}=\dfrac{1}{d}\left(cW-sU(U-m)(1-U)(U+V)+aUV\right),\\[6.45831pt] \dfrac{dR}{dz}=cR-bUV+gV(U+V).\end{array}\right.

Inspired by the biological origins of (2), we restrict our analysis of (2) to the set Ω={(U,V,W,R)∈ℝ4:U≥0,V≥0}\Omega=\{(U,V,W,R)\in\mathbb{R}^{4}:\,\,U\geq 0,V\geq 0\}. A traveling wave of (2) is any bounded solution of the system (2) contained in the domain Ω\Omega. These solutions are functions that “travel” in space, preserving their form as time goes by [23, 39, 38].

As we need to find bounded solutions of the system (2), we focus our attention on three special types of traveling waves: wave pulses, wave fronts, and wave trains [23]. Fig. 1(a) shows an actual homoclinic orbit of (2) found with the method presented later, in §5. The homoclinic orbit connects the equilibrium point 𝐪=(qu,qv,0,0)\mathbf{q}=(q_{u},q_{v},0,0) (given explicitly in §3) to itself. The homoclinic connection is an orbit in the unstable manifold of 𝐪\mathbf{q}, Wu​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{q}), that comes back to 𝐪\mathbf{q} along its stable manifold Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}), i.e., it is in the intersection Wu​(𝐪)∩Ws​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{q})\cap W^{s}(\mathbf{q}). The time series of UU and VV associated with this connecting orbit are shown in Fig. 1(b) in blue and orange, respectively. The profile of this solution is characterized by a large deviation (or pulse) in the amplitudes of UU and VV followed by a convergence back to the resting state. This corresponds to a wave pulse in the original system (2) that travels from a spatially homogeneous stationary solution to itself. Therefore, homoclinic orbits of (2) correspond to wave pulses of (2).

Fig. 2(a) shows a heteroclinic orbit connecting 𝐪\mathbf{q} to the equilibrium 𝐩=(pu,pv,0,0)\mathbf{p}=(p_{u},p_{v},0,0) (given explicitly below, in §3). The heteroclinic connection is an orbit in Wu​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{q}) which moves away from 𝐪\mathbf{q}, but it is also contained in the stable manifold of 𝐩\mathbf{p} Ws​(𝐩)W^{s}(\mathbf{p}), and hence, heads toward 𝐩\mathbf{p}. That is, this heteroclinic orbit lies in Wu​(𝐪)∩Ws​(𝐩)W^{u}(\mathbf{q})\cap W^{s}(\mathbf{p}). This corresponds to a wave of (2) that makes the transition from one spatially homogeneous stationary solution to another as is shown in Fig. 2(b).

The homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits (and their associated time series) as solutions of (2) are parameterized by z∈(−∞,∞)z\in(-\infty,\infty). However, for computational purposes, this independent variable is rescaled to z∈[0,1]z\in[0,1] in all our results; this is actually a standard procedure with numerical continuation methods (see [13, 28] and references therein). Moreover, in Fig. 1 (and for every other wave pulse shown throughout this paper) we restrict the values of zz to those compact subintervals of ]0,1[]0,1[ where the pulses are easier to see.

The third kind of wave solution of (2) we are interested in is wave trains. These solutions correspond to periodic orbits of system (2), as is illustrated in Fig. 3. For computational purposes, the period of every periodic orbit of (2) is rescaled to T=1T=1; see [13, 28]. In particular, in Fig. 3 (and for every other wave train shown throughout this paper) we restrict the values of zz to one such period of the cycle.

b32=a​gb​d​qu,b41=−(b−g)​qv,b42=(b−g)​qu.\displaystyle b_{32}=\dfrac{ag}{bd}q_{u},\,\quad b_{41}=-(b-g)q_{v},\,b_{42}=(b-g)q_{u}.

Hence, the computation of analytic expressions for the eigenvalues of D​X​(𝐩)DX(\mathbf{p}) and D​X​(𝐪)DX(\mathbf{q}) turns out to be a cumbersome goal. However, direct inspection of equilibrium coordinates reveals evidence of some local bifurcations. If b=gb=g, then from (14) we have that qv=pv=0q_{v}=p_{v}=0, qu=1q_{u}=1, and pu=mp_{u}=m, since

b​s​(1+m)±b2​s2​(m−1)22​b​s=1+m±(1−m)2.\displaystyle\dfrac{bs(1+m)\pm\sqrt{b^{2}s^{2}(m-1)^{2}}}{2bs}=\dfrac{1+m\pm(1-m)}{2}.

This implies that 𝐪=𝐩1\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p}_{1} and 𝐩=𝐩m\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{p}_{m}. Since, according to Lemma 1, there is a stability change for 𝐩1\mathbf{p}_{1} and 𝐩m\mathbf{p}_{m} when b=gb=g, this is an indication of a transcritical bifurcation. The equilibrium points 𝐪\mathbf{q} and 𝐩1\mathbf{p}_{1} collide and interchange their stability when b=gb=g; a similar statement follows for 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐩m\mathbf{p}_{m}. On the other hand, if Δ=0\Delta=0, then qu=puq_{u}=p_{u} and qv=pvq_{v}=p_{v}, so that 𝐪=𝐩\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p}. Since these two equilibria exist only if Δ>0\Delta>0, this is evidence of a saddle-node (or fold) bifurcation of equilibrium points. Formal proofs for these statements require the reduction of (2) into a one-parameter family of center manifolds on each case, followed by verification of certain genericity conditions; we refer to [21, 30] for more details. However, we opt to omit these proofs in favor of a focus on the analysis of global bifurcations in (2) and the emergence of traveling waves in (2).

4. Bifurcation analysis

In this section, we present a bifurcation analysis of (2) performed with the standard continuation package Auto. As a starting point, we consider parameters a=24a=24, b=19b=19, g=1g=1 and s=100s=100 fixed throughout this section and let dd and mm to vary. The fixed values of a,b,ga,b,g and ss correspond to those in [5] after the transformation (2). As in general the wave speed is a continuous function of the parameters system, i.e., c=c⁡(d,s,b,g,a,m)c=c(d,s,b,g,a,m), for the purpose of simplification we take the initial value c=1c=1 for the wave speed in (2). This approach can be thought of as an exploratory phase in which one navigates the possible preimages of c⁡(d,s,b,g,a,m)=1c(d,s,b,g,a,m)=1 in parameter space that allow solutions in the traveling frame of reference moving at speed c=1c=1. Later in §9, we let cc to vary in order to capture the existence and properties of the wave solutions by means of a wider range of preimage values of cc.

The resulting bifurcation scenario in the (m,d)(m,d)-plane is shown in Fig. 4. Of special importance for us are the curves hph_{p} and hqh_{q} which represent homoclinic bifurcations to 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐪\mathbf{q}, respectively. We will address the technical details and consequences of these homoclinic bifurcations later in §5. For the moment, it suffices to say that hph_{p} is divided into two segments (labeled as hpch_{p}^{c} and hpsh_{p}^{s}, respectively) by a codimension two Belyakov homoclinic point, labeled as BB [6, 7]. The right-hand side endpoints of both hpch_{p}^{c} and hqh_{q} (marked with ×\times) correspond to the last points where we could obtain convergence of the computed solutions with Auto.

Fig. 4 also shows a curve of Hopf bifurcation at the equilibrium 𝐩\mathbf{p}. This bifurcation curve is divided into two segments. The first one is a segment of supercritical Hopf bifurcation, labeled as Hp−H_{p}^{-}; the other one is a segment of subcritical Hopf bifurcation, labeled as Hp+H_{p}^{+}. The separation between both sides of the Hopf curve occurs at a codimension two Zero-Hopf bifurcation point (labeled as Z​HZH) where the Hopf curve meets a Fold bifurcation curve FF in a quadratic tangency. The curve labeled as P​DPD corresponds to a period doubling bifurcation, while N​SNS is a Neimark-Sacker (or torus) bifurcation curve. These two curves meet at a codimension two strong resonant point, R2R_{2}. The horizontal dotted line in Fig. 4 corresponds to d=1d=1 (or equivalently, D1=D2D_{1}=D_{2} in (1)). While this line does not represent any bifurcation, it is useful to distinguish the phenomena encountered above it from that which occurs below it. Indeed, one must remember that if d>1d>1 (resp. d<1d<1), then 𝐮\mathbf{u} has a higher (resp. lower) diffusion rate than 𝐯\mathbf{v}.

The bifurcation curves in Fig. 4 divide the (m,d)(m,d)-plane into the open regions I-VIII. Region VIII is bounded to the left by the curve FF, while I is delimited to its right by FF, and below by Hp−H_{p}^{-}. Region II is surrounded by the curves Hp−H_{p}^{-}, N​SNS, and P​DPD; while region III is enclosed by the curves P​DPD, hp+h_{p}^{+}, and hqh_{q}. Furthermore, region IV is bounded by the segments hqh_{q}, hp+h_{p}^{+}, and P​DPD, while region V is surrounded by the curves P​DPD, hp−h_{p}^{-}, and hp+h_{p}^{+}. Finally, region VI is enclosed by the curves hp−h_{p}^{-}, hp+h_{p}^{+}, P​DPD, N​SNS, and Hp+H_{p}^{+}, while region VII is delimited to the right by the curve FF and above by Hp+H_{p}^{+}.

It is relevant to note that the fold curve FF corresponds to the equation Δ=0\Delta=0 in §3. Hence, equilibrium points 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐪\mathbf{q} exist on the left-hand side of the FF curve (regions I-VII). In particular, if (m,d)∈I(m,d)\in{\rm I}, both equilibria are hyperbolic. If (m,d)(m,d) passes through the supercritical Hopf bifurcation curve Hp−H_{p}^{-} from region I towards region II, a limit cycle branches out from 𝐩\mathbf{p}. While the Hopf bifurcation is supercritical, this criticality is restricted only to a suitable two-dimensional center manifold where the bifurcation takes place [21, 30]; the resulting periodic orbit in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} is, in fact, of saddle type in region II. The stability properties of this cycle remain unchanged until this orbit undergoes a period doubling bifurcation when (m,d)∈P​D(m,d)\in PD. This periodic orbit faces a number of further bifurcations (not shown in Fig. 4) as the point (m,d)(m,d) moves towards the curve hqh_{q} where it gives rise to a homoclinic orbit. We will address this transition again in §6. On the other hand, when the point (m,d)(m,d) crosses the N​SNS curve from region II into region VI, an invariant torus bifurcates as a periodic orbit undergoes a Neimark-Sacker bifurcation.

Our bifurcation diagram in Fig. 4 is just partially complete. Other codimension two strong resonances can be found along the N​SNS bifurcation curve. Although the complete bifurcation diagram near these bifurcation points is yet to be known in its full complexity, one should expect the appearance of chaotic behavior when the point (m,d)(m,d) is in a neighborhood of the N​SNS curve; for further details, see [30]. Furthermore, bifurcation theory tells us that there is an infinite number of bifurcation curves in neighborhoods of both points BB and R2R_{2}. However, the full bifurcation picture near each of these points is not fully known from a theoretical point of view [30]. (We will address the complex dynamics that emerges due to the point BB in §5 below).

5. Homoclinic bifurcations, wave pulses, and chaos

Fig. 5 shows three different homoclinic orbits to the equilibrium 𝐩\mathbf{p} in the left-hand side column, and their corresponding time series in the right-hand side column. The values of parameters (m,d)(m,d) for each case correspond to those marked as ♢,\diamondsuit, □\Box and ×\times along the curve hph_{p} in Fig. 4. In the left-hand side column of Fig. 5, the homoclinic trajectories develop a rotational movement near 𝐩\mathbf{p} before making a large excursion and returning to 𝐩\mathbf{p}; see the sequence of panels (a1)-(b1)-(c1). The amplitude of these oscillations increases as the point (m,d)(m,d) moves to the right along the curve hph_{p}. As a result, the corresponding wave pulses in panels (a2)-(b2)-(c2) feature an initial transient with increasingly larger oscillations —as (m,d)(m,d) moves to the right along hph_{p}— around the equilibrium values; in each case, this culminates in a large pulse before decaying back to the rest state. Indeed, the initial pattern of smaller amplitude oscillations of each wave takes most of a long interval of values of z∈]0,1[z\in]0,1[ (i.e, it is a “slow” build-up in terms of zz); while the large amplitude pulse occurs in a smaller interval (of order 10−410^{-4}) of parameter zz (i.e, a “fast” discharge). Further, notice that both state variables 𝐮\mathbf{u} and 𝐯\mathbf{v} tend to increase and decrease simultaneously along any given traveling pulse.

The existence of the homoclinic orbit to 𝐩\mathbf{p} implies the presence of chaotic dynamics in (2). Let us now state the main reasons for this claim. For any (m,d)(m,d) in a neighbourhood of the curve hph_{p}, the linearization of (2) at the equilibrium 𝐩\mathbf{p} has one (stable) eigenvalue λs<0\lambda^{s}<0 and three (unstable) eigenvalues λ1,2u∈ℂ\lambda_{1,2}^{u}\in\mathbb{C}, and λ3u>0\lambda_{3}^{u}>0. In particular, λ1,2u\lambda_{1,2}^{u} are complex conjugate with positive real part Re⁡(λ1,2u)>0{\rm Re}(\lambda_{1,2}^{u})>0. The equilibrium 𝐩\mathbf{p} is called a saddle-focus. Fig. 6 shows all the possible values of the eigenvalues of 𝐩\mathbf{p} (in the complex plane) along the computed segment of the homoclinic bifurcation curve hph_{p}. Namely, as parameters (m,d)(m,d) are allowed to vary along the computed segment of the curve hph_{p} in Fig. 4, each eigenvalue of 𝐩\mathbf{p} traces out a curve segment whose plots are shown in Fig. 6. Among the unstable eigenvalues, the pair λ1,2u\lambda_{1,2}^{u} are the closest to the imaginary axis Re⁡(λ)=0{\rm Re}(\lambda)=0; hence, we say that λ1,2u\lambda_{1,2}^{u} are the leading unstable eigenvalues. In this setting, if we define the so-called saddle quantity as σ1=λs+Re⁡(λ1,2u)\sigma_{1}=\lambda^{s}+{\rm Re}(\lambda_{1,2}^{u}), Shilnikov’s theorems [21, 30, 48, 49] state that if σ1>0\sigma_{1}>0, the homoclinic bifurcation is simple or mild. In this simple Shilnikov homoclinic bifurcation, a single (repelling) periodic orbit bifurcates from the homoclinic orbit on one side of the curve hph_{p}. On the other hand, if σ1<0\sigma_{1}<0, the homoclinic bifurcation is chaotic and gives rise to a wide range of complicated behavior in phase space. More specifically, one can find horseshoe dynamics in return maps defined in a neighbourhood of the homoclinic orbit. The suspension of the Smale horsehoes forms a hyperbolic invariant chaotic set which contains countably many periodic orbits of saddle-type. The horseshoe dynamics is robust under small parameter perturbations, i.e., the chaotic dynamics persist even when the homoclinic connection is broken; see [21, 30]. The segments labeled as hpsh_{p}^{s} and hpch_{p}^{c} in Fig. 4 correspond to simple and chaotic regimes, respectively, and are separated by the Belyakov point BB where σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0 [6, 7]. (Actually, at (m,d)=B(m,d)=B, we have Re⁡(λ1,2u)=|λs|≈0.6654466{\rm Re}(\lambda^{u}_{1,2})=|\lambda^{s}|\approx 0.6654466). Likewise, in Fig. 6, the segments hpsh_{p}^{s} and hpch_{p}^{c} along the curves for λ1,2u\lambda_{1,2}^{u} correspond to σ1>0\sigma_{1}>0 (simple) and σ1<0\sigma_{1}<0 (chaotic), respectively, and are separated by the point labeled as BB where σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0. This same Belyakov transition is shown for the corresponding λs\lambda^{s} value as well (and is also labeled as BB).

The bifurcation picture near the curve hph_{p} in Fig. 4 is just a partial representation of the full complexity one may encounter in this region of parameter space. Indeed, the saddle periodic orbits associated with the invariant chaotic set may also undergo further bifurcations such as period-doubling and torus bifurcations [21, 30]. Moreover, the presence of the chaotic hpch_{p}^{c} bifurcation and that of the Belyakov point BB imply a very complicated structure (not shown) of infinitely many saddle-node and period-doubling bifurcations of periodic orbits as well as of subsidiary nn-homoclinic orbits. Fig. 7 shows a 2-homoclinic orbit to 𝐩\mathbf{p} (in panel (a1)) and a 4-homoclinic orbit to 𝐩\mathbf{p} (in panel (b1)), as well as their corresponding time series in panels (a2) and (b2), respectively. In general, nn-homoclinic orbits are characterized by making n−1n-1 close passes near the equilibrium before closing up to form the connection; see panels (a1) and (b1). As a consequence, the corresponding traveling wave develops nn pulses before setting down to the steady state values; see the 2-pulse and 4-pulse waves in panels (a1) and (b1), respectively. Moreover, for each of these subsidiary nn-homoclinic orbits, the system exhibits horseshoe dynamics and chaos as in the original homoclinic scenario.

As for the homoclinic bifurcation hqh_{q} at the equilibrium 𝐪\mathbf{q}, the associated Jacobian matrix of (2) at 𝐪\mathbf{q} has a pair of complex-conjugate stable eigenvalues μ1,2s∈ℂ\mu_{1,2}^{s}\in\mathbb{C} and a pair of complex-conjugate unstable eigenvalues μ1,2u∈ℂ\mu_{1,2}^{u}\in\mathbb{C}, with Re⁡(μ1,2s)<0{\rm Re}(\mu_{1,2}^{s})<0 and Re⁡(μ1,2u)>0{\rm Re}(\mu_{1,2}^{u})>0. The structure of the eigenvalues of 𝐪\mathbf{q} as a function of (m,d)∈hq(m,d)\in h_{q} is shown in Fig. 8. We say that 𝐪\mathbf{q} is a focus-focus or bi-focus. The resulting homoclinic orbit Γq\Gamma_{q} features a spiral-type convergence to 𝐪\mathbf{q} as z→±∞z\rightarrow\pm\infty. Fig. 9 shows three different examples of such homoclinic orbit in the left column, and their respective time series in the right one. The values of parameters (m,d)(m,d) for each case correspond to those marked as ♢,\diamondsuit, □\Box and ×\times along the curve hqh_{q} in Fig. 4. In the left-hand side column of Fig. 9, the amplitude of the oscillations increases as the point (m,d)(m,d) moves to the right along the curve hqh_{q}. As a result, the corresponding wave pulses in panels (a2)-(b2)-(c2) develop more oscillations —as (m,d)(m,d) moves to the right along hqh_{q}— before converging to the equilibrium values as z→∞z\rightarrow\infty. The spirals and oscillations that are visible in panels (a1)-(b1)-(c1) and in panels (a2)-(b2)-(c2), respectively, are associated with the stable eigenvalues μ1,2s\mu_{1,2}^{s} of 𝐪\mathbf{q}. There is another set of oscillations as z→−∞z\rightarrow-\infty which are associated with the unstable eigenvalues μ1,2u\mu_{1,2}^{u}; however, since Im⁡(μ1,2u)<Im⁡(μ1,2s){\rm Im}(\mu_{1,2}^{u})<{\rm Im}(\mu_{1,2}^{s}) (see Fig. 8 again), these spirals are relatively less pronounced and hard to see in Fig. 9. Nevertheless, like the case of the homoclinic orbit to 𝐩\mathbf{p}, here both 𝐮\mathbf{u} and 𝐯\mathbf{v} tend to increase and decrease simultaneously along any given traveling pulse.

The homoclinic bifurcation at the focus-focus equilibrium 𝐪\mathbf{q} induces chaotic dynamics for every (m,d)∈hq(m,d)\in h_{q}. Indeed, the presence of the homoclinic orbit Γq\Gamma_{q} to a focus-focus equilibrium is accompanied by horseshoe dynamics in cross sections near Γq\Gamma_{q} and, hence, an infinite number of saddle periodic orbits in a neighbourhood of Γq\Gamma_{q} [30, 41]. Furthermore, in this setting, the saddle quantity is defined as σ2=Re⁡(μ1,2s)+Re⁡(μ1,2u)\sigma_{2}={\rm Re}(\mu_{1,2}^{s})+{\rm Re}(\mu_{1,2}^{u}). Since σ2>0\sigma_{2}>0 for every (m,d)∈hq(m,d)\in h_{q}, it follows that there are no stable periodic orbits near Γq\Gamma_{q} [19, 23].

In sum, any solution in a neighborhood of either Γp\Gamma_{p} (in the chaotic case) or Γq\Gamma_{q} tends to behave erratically and presents sensitive dependence to initial conditions. The corresponding orbit in the four-dimensional phase space of (2) spends a long transient visiting a strange hyperbolic invariant set before converging to an attractor. Hence, any bounded solution of (2) passing near either Γp\Gamma_{p} (in the hpch_{p}^{c} side of the bifurcation) or Γq\Gamma_{q} is associated with a chaotic traveling wave [41].

Fig. 10(a) shows both homoclinic orbits Γp\Gamma_{p} and Γq\Gamma_{q} coexisting in phase space, while Fig. 10(b1) and Fig. 10(b2) show the time series of UU and VV associated with either trajectory. This special configuration occurs when the bifurcation curves hpch_{p}^{c} and hqh_{q} cross each other at (m,d)≈(0.046336476,1.11668)(m,d)\approx(0.046336476,1.11668); see the bifurcation diagram of Fig. 4. While this intersection point is not a new bifurcation, at these parameter values both classes of homoclinic orbits, Γq\Gamma_{q} and Γp\Gamma_{p}, coexist in phase space. Moreover, one obtains the coexistence of both chaotic invariant sets (each associated with one of the homoclinic trajectories) and, hence, the corresponding erratic behavior and sensitive dependence on initial conditions of nearby solutions.

6. Periodic orbits and wave trains

In this section we study the limit cycles existing in (2), their bifurcations, and their consequences for the nature of wave trains.

6.1. Period doubling phenomena

Let us consider the periodic orbit Γ\Gamma which originates at the supercritical Hopf bifurcation Hp−H_{p}^{-} and track its successive bifurcations as parameter dd is decreased and m=0.0463358m=0.0463358 remains fixed. When (m,d)(m,d) crosses the P​DPD curve from region II to III, the cycle Γ\Gamma undergoes a period doubling bifurcation. As (m,d)(m,d) enters region III, Γ\Gamma changes its stability and a secondary limit cycle Γ2\Gamma^{2} appears with approximately twice the period of Γ\Gamma. As parameter dd is further decreased, additional period doubling events occur (not shown in Fig. 4). This is illustrated in Fig. 11. Periodic orbits Γ2\Gamma^{2}, Γ4\Gamma^{4} and Γ8\Gamma^{8} of periods 2, 4, and 8 times that of Γ\Gamma, respectively, are shown in panels (a1)-(b1)-(c1). Panels (a2)-(b2)-(c2) show one period of the corresponding time series of UU and VV. Here, the actual periods of the solutions are rescaled to T=1T=1 for visualization and computational purposes [13]. As a consequence, as parameter dd decreases and system (2) undergoes this sequence of period doubling bifurcations, the associated wave trains in panels (a2)-(b2)-(c2) display periodic patterns with doubling periods.

6.2. Transition from wave trains to wave pulses

It is essential to highlight that when the point (m,d)(m,d) crosses the PD curve from region II to region III, the cycle Γ\Gamma does not disappear but just changes its stability. Fig. 12 shows the graph of the period TT of this cycle as a function of dd. The bifurcation curve oscillates around the critical value d∗≈1.3080156d^{*}\approx 1.3080156 for which the homoclinic bifurcation hqh_{q} to 𝐪\mathbf{q} occurs. The amplitude of the oscillations decreases rapidly as the homoclinic limit is approached when dd tends to d∗d^{*}; see [30] and references therein. Indeed, the “snaking” behavior of the bifurcation curve is typical of the main branch of periodic orbits near chaotic saddle-focus and focus-focus homoclinic bifurcations [19, 52]. At each of the infinitely many folds of the curve, a pair of periodic orbits is created via a saddle-node bifurcation of limit cycles. Some of the periodic orbits in this branch may further undergo period-doubling bifurcations changing their stability along the bifurcation curve. Fig. 13 shows three such periodic orbits, labelled as ΓA\Gamma_{A}, ΓB\Gamma_{B}, and ΓC\Gamma_{C}, respectively, corresponding to the points AA, BB and CC in Fig. 12. As dd approaches d∗d^{*}, the cycles pass increasingly closer to 𝐪\mathbf{q} (see the sequence of panels (a1)-(b1)-(c1) in Fig. 13). As a result, one obtains wave trains which spend longer transients close to the equilibrium values (see the sequence of panels (a2)-(b2)-(c2) in which the period TT of each cycle is rescaled to 1). Hence, one can think of the homoclinic orbit Γq\Gamma_{q} (and its corresponding wave pulse) as the limit of this sequence of periodic orbits (resp. wave trains) of increasing period as d→d∗d\rightarrow d^{*}. Furthermore, each of the periodic orbits bifurcated from the period doubling phenomena in subsection 6.1 may also increase their periods and undergo a convergence to nn-homoclinic orbits in a similar fashion. Some of these secondary homoclinic bifurcations are mentioned before in §5 and shown in Fig. 7.

7. Heteroclinic connections and wave fronts

Fig. 14(a) shows a heteroclinic orbit, labeled as Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p}, obtained for (m,d)=(0.0463358,2.4)(m,d)=(0.0463358,2.4) in region I. The heteroclinic connection is oriented from 𝐪\mathbf{q} to 𝐩\mathbf{p} as parameter zz —that which parametrizes the curve— is increased. The resulting time series are shown in Fig. 14(b), and they correspond to a wave front traveling from the steady state 𝐪\mathbf{q} that decays exponentially to 𝐩\mathbf{p} in synchronized oscillatory fashion. This non-monotonic behavior is explained by the presence of a pair of stable complex-conjugate eigenvalues (with negative real part) of 𝐩\mathbf{p} when parameters (m,d)(m,d) are in region I. The connecting orbit Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p} lies in the intersection of the global invariant manifolds Ws​(𝐩)W^{s}(\mathbf{p}) and Wu​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{q}). Namely, Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p} is contained in the two-dimensional unstable manifold Wu​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{q}) —represented in Fig. 14(a) as a transparent red surface— and approaches 𝐩\mathbf{p} along its three-dimensional stable manifold Ws​(𝐩)W^{s}(\mathbf{p}) (not shown). Moreover, since Ws​(𝐩)W^{s}(\mathbf{p}) and Wu​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{q}) are, respectively, three and two-dimensional immersed smooth manifolds in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}, one may anticipate that the intersection Ws​(𝐩)∩Wu​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{p})\cap W^{u}(\mathbf{q}) will generically be transverse [22]. Indeed, this is in agreement with the fact that Ws​(𝐩)∩Wu​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{p})\cap W^{u}(\mathbf{q}) corresponds to a one-dimensional object in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}. Hence, one may reliably expect the heteroclinic orbit Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p} and, hence, its associated wave front to persist under small parameter variations: The resulting wave front may vary the amplitude of its oscillations and the actual asymptotic values, but the qualitative behavior of the traveling front remains unaltered throughout.

As parameter (m,d)(m,d) crosses the Hp−H_{p}^{-} curve from region I to region II, a pair of stable eigenvalues of 𝐩\mathbf{p} cross the imaginary axis and become unstable; in the process, a limit cycle branches from 𝐩\mathbf{p} in a supercritical Hopf bifurcation. Hence, in region II, Ws​(𝐩)W^{s}(\mathbf{p}) is a one-dimensional manifold and the connection Γq,p\Gamma_{q,p} does not exist. Rather, it is replaced by a heteroclinic orbit that joins 𝐪\mathbf{q} to the bifurcated cycle. Fig. 15(a) shows the bifurcated periodic orbit, labeled as γ\gamma after (m,d)(m,d) has entered region II from region I. The unstable manifold Wu​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{q}) (red surface) rolls up around γ\gamma and intersects the three-dimensional stable manifold Ws​(γ)W^{s}(\gamma) (not shown) transversally along a heteroclinic orbit, labeled as Γq,γ\Gamma_{q,\gamma}. This heteroclinic connection is associated with the traveling wave shown in Fig. 15(b); this is a front transitioning from the steady state at 𝐪\mathbf{q} into a periodic pattern around 𝐩\mathbf{p}. The heteroclinic orbit Γq,γ\Gamma_{q,\gamma} (and its traveling front) is preserved in an open subset of region II, and it disappears when (m,d)(m,d) crosses the PD curve towards region III as γ\gamma loses its stability in a period doubling bifurcation.

If (m,d)(m,d) is in an open subset of regions III, IV, and V, one can find a wave front traveling from 𝐩\mathbf{p} to 𝐪\mathbf{q}. This front travels in the opposite direction to that in Fig. 14 and, hence, it corresponds to a third kind of wave. The wave front traveling from 𝐩\mathbf{p} to 𝐪\mathbf{q} is shown in Fig. 16(b). The wave begins at the steady state 𝐩\mathbf{p} with oscillations of increasing amplitude until it settles at 𝐪\mathbf{q}. This front corresponds to an intersection of the manifolds Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}) and Wu​(𝐩)W^{u}(\mathbf{p}) forming a heteroclinic orbit in the phase space of (2); Fig. 16(a) shows the heteroclinic orbit (labelled as Γp,q\Gamma_{p,q}) and the two-dimensional manifold Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}) of 𝐪\mathbf{q} as a transparent blue surface. The connection Γp,q\Gamma_{p,q} is an orbit in the three dimensional unstable manifold Wu​(𝐩)W^{u}(\mathbf{p}) which lies on Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}) to converge to 𝐪\mathbf{q}.

8. Multiple wave fronts at the focus-focus homoclinic bifurcation

In §5, we described the complicated dynamics that can be found near the focus-focus homoclinic bifurcation Γq\Gamma_{q} when (m,d)∈hq(m,d)\in h_{q}. One of the consequences of this fact is the appearance of multiple wave fronts of type Γp,q\Gamma_{p,q} (described in §7) which coexist with the main wave pulse Γq\Gamma_{q}. We explain this finding here by direct, close inspection of the invariant manifolds involved.

Fig. 17 shows the projection of Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}) onto the U​V​WUVW space, when

(m,d)≈(0.0463358,1.3080156)∈hq.(m,d)\approx(0.0463358,1.3080156)\in h_{q}.

Also shown is the homoclinic orbit Γq\Gamma_{q} (red curve). The two-dimensional manifold Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}) is rendered as a transparent blue surface. Some orbits in Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}) lie in the three-dimensional unstable manifold Wu​(𝐩)W^{u}(\mathbf{p}) forming heteroclinic connections. In our computations, we detected seven heteroclinic orbits contained in Wu​(𝐩)∩Ws​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{p})\cap W^{s}(\mathbf{q}). Most of these heteroclinic connections are very close to one another and very hard to distinguish from each other; we show one of them (cyan curve labeled as Γp,q\Gamma_{p,q}) in Fig. 17. Each of these seven heteroclinic orbits corresponds to a different wave front traveling from 𝐩\mathbf{p} to 𝐪\mathbf{q}, which are present in the system at the same time.

Further, there are also 2- and 3-homoclinic orbits to 𝐪\mathbf{q} in Wu​(𝐪)∩Ws​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{q})\cap W^{s}(\mathbf{q}), coexisting with the primary homoclinic orbit and the heteroclinic connections in phase space; we opted to not show these subsidiary homoclinic orbits in Fig. 17 for visualization purposes. Fig. 18(a) shows the profiles of UU associated with the primary wave pulse Γq\Gamma_{q} and the secondary 2- and 3-pulse waves (labeled as Γq2\Gamma_{q}^{2} and Γq3\Gamma_{q}^{3}, respectively) associated with the secondary homoclinic orbits. In turn, Fig. 18(b) shows three representative traveling fronts associated with the family of heteroclinic orbits in phase space. The existence of these families of wave fronts when (m,d)∈hq(m,d)\in h_{q} indicates that there must be a sequence of associated global bifurcations as (m,d)(m,d) approaches the hqh_{q} curve. At each of these bifurcation events, the manifolds Wu​(𝐩)W^{u}(\mathbf{p}) and Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}) intersect tangentially in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} along a (newly created) heteroclinic orbit. As (m,d)(m,d) moves closer to the hqh_{q} curve, the intersection becomes transversal and the heteroclinic orbit persists under small parameter variations. Similar events happen in the case of the secondary homoclinic orbits in the intersection of Wu​(𝐪)W^{u}(\mathbf{q}) and Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}), that explain the emergence of 2- and 3-pulse waves as parameters (m,d)(m,d) approach the hqh_{q} curve.

The method to detect these connections is explained as follows. If Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}) contains a heteroclinic orbit flowing from 𝐩\mathbf{p} to 𝐪\mathbf{q}, such trajectory is approximated by a bounded solution contained in a family W^δ,Ts​(𝐪)\widehat{W}^{s}_{\delta,T}(\mathbf{q}) of orbit segments passing sufficiently close to 𝐩\mathbf{p} and satisfying a two-point boundary value problem. Every solution in W^δ,Ts​(𝐪)\widehat{W}^{s}_{\delta,T}(\mathbf{q}) is continued up to an integration time TT (which is a free parameter in this continuation) and is parametrized by a unique location δ∈[0,1)\delta\in[0,1) in a fundamental domain; see [4, 6, 28] for more details. Indeed, if a heteroclinic orbit exists, the two-parameter continuation procedure effectively stops as the integration time diverges. In practice, an approximation of such connecting orbit is obtained at some specific δ=δ∗∈[0,1)\delta=\delta^{*}\in[0,1) with a large integration time T=−T∗T=-T^{*}. A similar criterium can be used to detect secondary nn-homoclinic orbits to 𝐪\mathbf{q} as orbit segments ending near 𝐪\mathbf{q} as the integration time TT diverges. For instance, in Fig. 17 and Fig. 18, the fundamental domain δ∈[0,1)\delta\in[0,1) is divided into 13 sub-segments by the values 0<δ1<δ2<…<δ12<10<\delta_{1}<\delta_{2}<\ldots<\delta_{12}<1. The heteroclinic connections correspond to δ1≈0.317181\delta_{1}\approx 0.317181, δ2≈0.317265\delta_{2}\approx 0.317265, δ6≈0.319579\delta_{6}\approx 0.319579, δ8≈0.319621\delta_{8}\approx 0.319621, δ9≈0.319904\delta_{9}\approx 0.319904, δ11≈0.319917\delta_{11}\approx 0.319917 and δ12≈0.331911\delta_{12}\approx 0.331911. On the other hand, we have the primary homoclinic orbit at δ7≈0.319616\delta_{7}\approx 0.319616, and four secondary homoclinic orbits at δ3≈0.317284\delta_{3}\approx 0.317284, δ4≈0.317285\delta_{4}\approx 0.317285, δ5≈0.317285\delta_{5}\approx 0.317285 and δ10≈0.319906.\delta_{10}\approx 0.319906.

9. The influence of propagation speed and diffusion ratio

The study and results reported so far in sections 4–8 were produced with fixed wave speed c=1c=1. Here we ask ourselves if there is a minimum wave speed needed for the existence of some of the traveling waves we have found. To this end, we consider the homoclinic orbits Γp\Gamma_{p} and Γq\Gamma_{q} existing at the curves hph_{p} and hqh_{q}, respectively, when m≈0.0463358m\approx 0.0463358, and continue them in parameters cc and dd. Fig. 19 shows the homoclinic bifurcation curves hph_{p} and hqh_{q} in the (c,d)(c,d)-plane. The existence of both homoclinic orbits is determined by a positive correlation between the wave speed cc and the diffusion ratio dd; namely, as cc decreases, the wave pulses exist provided dd becomes sufficiently small.

In the case of hph_{p}, the relation between cc and dd in Fig. 19 is almost linear for c≥0.1c\geq 0.1. Indeed the curve hph_{p} can be approximated as d≈0.2925828​c+0.4333269,d\approx 0.2925828c+0.4333269, for 0.1≤c<10.1\leq c<1, with a root mean square error e=0.00521e=0.00521. In particular, the computed segment of the curve hph_{p} is located in the halfspace d<1d<1. Hence, this kind of pulse wave with small wave speed c<1c<1 occurs only if VV propagates in a more efficient way than UU. On the other hand, as cc decreases below 0.010.01, the diffusion ratio dd drops abruptly in a non linear way in the form d=𝒪⁡(c1/2)d=\mathcal{O}(c^{1/2}); see Fig. 19(c). As cc is further decreased, the continuation procedure loses precision and the last point where we get convergence of the numerical scheme is at cmin=0.0016767c_{\rm min}=0.0016767. Fig. 20 shows the homoclinic orbit Γp\Gamma_{p} when (c,d)=(0.0479321,0.4449391)(c,d)=(0.0479321,0.4449391) in panel (a), and its corresponding time series in panel (b). In panel (a), the orbit Γp\Gamma_{p} performs many low-amplitude turns in Wlocu​(𝐩)W^{u}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbf{p}) before developing the long excursion. The corresponding wave in panel (b) shows a slow pattern (in terms of zz) of small amplitude oscillations followed by a fast large amplitude pulse in a small interval (of order 10−410^{-4}) of parameter zz, similar to typical dynamic behaviors with different time scales. Indeed, if the relation d=𝒪⁡(c1/2)d=\mathcal{O}(c^{1/2}) still holds for c→0c\to 0, then both (2) and (2) become singular as c→0c\rightarrow 0 and d→0d\rightarrow 0; while these systems in the singular limit may be studied with tools from geometric singular perturbation theory [18], this is beyond the scope of this work. Nevertheless, solutions u⁡(x,t)=U⁡(x+c​t)u(x,t)=U(x+ct), v⁡(x,t)=V⁡(x+c​t)v(x,t)=V(x+ct) of (2) as c→0c\to 0 and d=D1/D2→0d=D_{1}/D_{2}\rightarrow 0 correspond to stationary waves in which, effectively, only the propagation of VV is observable in the length scale xx.

As for the bifurcation curve hqh_{q} in Fig. 19(a)-(b), the dependence between cc and dd is approximately quadratic. That is, a homoclinic orbit to the focus-focus 𝐪\mathbf{q} exists whenever cc and dd satisfy d≈0.0437881​c2−0.0016566​c+1.2656854d\approx 0.0437881c^{2}-0.0016566c+1.2656854, for 0≤c≤10\leq c\leq 1; the root mean square error of this approximation is e=6.8×10−5e=6.8\times 10^{-5}. In particular, the computed segment of the curve hqh_{q} is located in the half-space d>1d>1. Hence, this kind of pulse wave with small wave speed c<1c<1 occurs only if UU propagates in a more efficient way than VV. Moreover, the numerical evidence suggests that a pulse wave exists for every c>0c>0 arbitrarily small, i.e., there is no positive minimum value for the wave speed cc. Indeed, the bifurcation curve hqh_{q} can be continued down to cmin=0c_{\rm min}=0 with dmin≈1.2656854d_{\rm min}\approx 1.2656854. (In particular, the value dmin>0d_{\rm min}>0 prevents (2) and (2) to become singular, unlike the case of hph_{p}). In the limit as c→0c\rightarrow 0, the resulting wave pulse corresponds to a stationary solution of (2) where both state variables UU and VV propagate with diffusion ratio D1/D2=dminD_{1}/D_{2}=d_{\rm min}.

10. Traveling waves restricted to invariant planes

System (2) has two invariant planes given by

ΠU={(U,V,W,R)∈ℝ4:V=R=0},\Pi_{U}=\{(U,V,W,R)\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\ :\ V=R=0\},

and

ΠV={(U,V,W,R)∈ℝ4:U=W=0}.\Pi_{V}=\{(U,V,W,R)\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\ :\ U=W=0\}.

Note that the origin 𝐩0∈ΠU∩ΠV\mathbf{p}_{0}\in\Pi_{U}\cap\Pi_{V}. The restriction of (2) to ΠU\Pi_{U} is given by

XU:{d​Ud​z=W,d​Wd​z=1d​(c​W−s​U2​(U−m)​(1−U)).\displaystyle X_{U}:\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\dfrac{dU}{dz}=W,\\[6.45831pt] \dfrac{dW}{dz}=\dfrac{1}{d}\left(cW-sU^{2}(U-m)(1-U)\right).\end{array}\right.

System (10) has three equilibria: 𝟎=(0,0)\mathbf{0}=(0,0), (m,0)(m,0) and (1,0)(1,0), which correspond to the restrictions of 𝐩0\mathbf{p}_{0}, 𝐩m\mathbf{p}_{m} and 𝐩1\mathbf{p}_{1}, respectively, to ΠU\Pi_{U}. The equilibrium (m,0)(m,0) is a hyperbolic repeller and (1,0)(1,0) is a hyperbolic saddle of (10). This result is a direct consequence of Hartman-Grobman theorem. Indeed, the linear part of (10) is given by

D​XU​(U,W)=(01sd​(4​U3−3​(m+1)​U2+2​m​U)cd).\displaystyle DX_{U}(U,W)=\begin{pmatrix}0&&1\\ \dfrac{s}{d}\left(4U^{3}-3(m+1)U^{2}+2mU\right)&&\dfrac{c}{d}\end{pmatrix}.

Therefore, evaluation of D​XUDX_{U} at (m,0)(m,0) and (1,0)(1,0) is given, respectively, by

D​XU​(m,0)=(01sd​m2​(m−1)cd),D​XU​(1,0)=(01sd​(1−m)cd).\displaystyle DX_{U}(m,0)=\begin{pmatrix}0&&1\\ \dfrac{s}{d}m^{2}(m-1)&&\dfrac{c}{d}\end{pmatrix},\qquad DX_{U}(1,0)=\begin{pmatrix}0&&1\\ \dfrac{s}{d}(1-m)&&\dfrac{c}{d}\end{pmatrix}.

Furthermore, the eigenvalues of D​XU​(m,0)DX_{U}(m,0) and D​XU​(1,0)DX_{U}(1,0) are given, respectively, by

λ±m=c±c2−4​s​d​m2​(1−m)2​d,λ±1=c±c2+4​s​d​(1−m)2​d.\displaystyle\lambda_{\pm}^{m}=\dfrac{c\pm\sqrt{c^{2}-4sdm^{2}(1-m)}}{2d},\qquad\lambda_{\pm}^{1}=\dfrac{c\pm\sqrt{c^{2}+4sd(1-m)}}{2d}.

Since 0<m<10<m<1, then we have c2−4​s​d​m2​(1−m)<c2.c^{2}-4sdm^{2}(1-m)<c^{2}. Therefore, Re⁡(λ±m)>0{\rm Re}(\lambda_{\pm}^{m})>0 and, hence, this proves that (m,0)(m,0) is a repeller. On the other hand, note that c2+4​s​d​(1−m)>c2c^{2}+4sd(1-m)>c^{2}, so λ−1<0<λ+1\lambda_{-}^{1}<0<\lambda_{+}^{1}. Thus, (1,0)(1,0) is a saddle.

In the case of the origin (0,0)(0,0) of (10), we have

D​XU​(𝟎)=(010cd),\displaystyle DX_{U}(\mathbf{0})=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 0&\dfrac{c}{d}\end{pmatrix},

with associated eigenvalues λ10=0,\lambda_{1}^{0}=0, and λ20=c/d>0.\lambda_{2}^{0}=c/d>0. Hence, 𝟎\mathbf{0} is a non-hyperbolic equilibrium. The eigenvectors of D​XU​(𝟎)DX_{U}(\mathbf{0}) associated with λ10\lambda_{1}^{0} and λ20\lambda_{2}^{0} are v10=(1,0)Tv_{1}^{0}=(1,0)^{T} and v20=(c,d)Tv_{2}^{0}=(c,d)^{T}, respectively. According to the centre manifold theorem [21], the origin of (10) has a one-dimensional local centre manifold Wlocc​(𝟎)W_{\text{loc}}^{c}(\mathbf{0}) which is tangent to v10v_{1}^{0} at 𝟎\mathbf{0}. This implies that Wlocc​(𝟎)W_{\text{loc}}^{c}(\mathbf{0}) can be represented locally as the graph of a function W=W⁡(U)W=W(U) that satisfies W⁡(0)=W′​(0)=0W(0)=W^{\prime}(0)=0 (for further details, see [30]). By taking the Taylor series expansion of this function around U=0U=0, we have

W⁡(U)=∑k=2rak​Uk+𝒪⁡(Ur+1),W(U)=\sum_{k=2}^{r}a_{k}U^{k}+\mathcal{O}(U^{r+1}),

where the coefficients ak∈ℝa_{k}\in\mathbb{R}, and 𝒪⁡(Ur+1)\mathcal{O}(U^{r+1}) are terms of order r+1r+1 and higher of the Taylor series of W⁡(U)W(U). Here, the coefficients aka_{k} are determined by substitution of W=W⁡(U)W=W(U) into (10). Thus, after some calculations, we obtain

W⁡(U)=−m​sc​U2+𝒪⁡(U3).W(U)=-\dfrac{ms}{c}U^{2}+\mathcal{O}(U^{3}).

If we restrict (10) to Wlocc​(𝟎)W_{\text{loc}}^{c}(\mathbf{0}), we obtain the scalar differential equation

U′=W⁡(U)=−m​sc​U2+𝒪⁡(U3).\displaystyle U^{\prime}=W(U)=-\dfrac{ms}{c}U^{2}+\mathcal{O}(U^{3}).

Then, for U>0U>0 small enough, we have that U′<0U^{\prime}<0. Therefore, 𝟎\mathbf{0} is a local attractor in Wlocc​(𝟎)W_{\text{loc}}^{c}(\mathbf{0}). Since λ20>0\lambda_{2}^{0}>0, it follows that 𝟎\mathbf{0} is a non-hyperbolic saddle point of (10).

Fig. 21 shows the phase portrait of (10). The global centre manifold Wc​(𝟎)W^{c}(\mathbf{0}) extends itself (for z<0z<0) along the flow of (10) and forms a heteroclinic connection to (m,0)(m,0). This corresponds to a wave front in (2) in which v≡0v\equiv 0 and u→0u\rightarrow 0 as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. Moreover, since Wu​(m,0)W^{u}(m,0) is a two-dimensional unstable manifold, the intersection along Wc​(𝟎)∩Wu​(m,0)W^{c}(\mathbf{0})\cap W^{u}(m,0) is transversal. It follows that the associated wave front persists under small parameter variations. Notice that, under suitable parameter perturbations, the manifolds Wu​(𝟎)W^{u}(\mathbf{0}) and Ws​(1,0)W^{s}(1,0) may come to intersect along a second heteroclinic orbit from (0,0)(0,0) to (1,0)(1,0). Since this manifold intersection is non-transversal, the resulting heteroclinic orbit is structurally unstable, i.e., it might be broken under small parameter variation. However, the front itself could still persist in the PDE (2), but perhaps with a slightly adjusted speed cc.

Finally, a similar analysis of (2) restricted to the invariant plane ΠV\Pi_{V} reveals that there are either no homoclinic, heteroclinic orbits nor limit cycles with non-negative VV-coordinates in ΠV\Pi_{V}.

11. Discussion

We have investigated a diffusive process in a qualitative model (1) inspired by some minimal mathematical ingredients of a rescaled predator-prey interaction from [5]. Our goal was to undertake a systematic identification of traveling waves that may be encountered when the kinetic terms —based on those in [5]— are stated in their most elementary form. In particular, the analysis was performed searching for traveling wave solutions with strictly non-negative (u,v)(u,v) coordinates. While the considered system may rise some questions regarding its interpretability, this “prototype model” may be understood in the same spirit as investigating a sort of topological normal form: namely, if the kinetic terms are presented in their most reduced (and yet mathematically meaningful) form, what can one expect in terms of spatiotemporal behavior if diffusion is taken care of. Nevertheless, upon taking these observations into consideration, we opted not to call variables uu and vv as “prey” and “predator”, respectively, in order to avoid misleading conclusions and interpretations of our results.

In (1) the three main types of traveling waves we were looking for appear: wave pulses, wave fronts, and wave trains. Table 1 shows a list of all the traveling waves exposed throughout this paper, together with the regions of the bifurcation diagram in Fig. 4 where they can be found. We highlight that we made this table according to the obtained information, and the mentioned regions may not be the only ones where the given traveling waves can be found. Regarding the diffusion process, we found the condition d>1d>1 favors the presence of chaotic orbits in the traveling frame, i.e., the associated ODE system (2) is more likely to be chaotic when DuD_{u} is higher than DvD_{v}. Specifically, we can find chaos when (m,d)(m,d) lies in the neighborhood of the hph_{p}, hqh_{q} curves (homoclinic chaos) and the Neimark-Sacker curve N​SNS in the bifurcation diagram; see also the discussion in §5.

It is relevant to remember that there are regions where two or more types of traveling waves exist simultaneously. For example, if (m,d)(m,d) is in the intersection between hqh_{q} and hph_{p}, then there are two homoclinic orbits, Γq\Gamma_{q} and Γp\Gamma_{p}. Furthermore, let us remember that Γ2\Gamma^{2} is branched from Γ\Gamma when (m,d)(m,d) crosses the period-doubling curve P​DPD from region II to III. However, Γ\Gamma does not disappear after this event. In fact, after the successive period doubling bifurcations, a large number of wave trains may be found together in the phase portrait of system (2). Finally, we should recall that when (m,d)≈(0.0463358,1.3080156)∈hq(m,d)\approx(0.0463358,1.3080156)\in h_{q}, there is a family of heteroclinic orbits, which go from 𝐩\mathbf{p} to 𝐪\mathbf{q}. These arise from a transverse intersection between Wu​(𝐩)W^{u}(\mathbf{p}) and Ws​(𝐪)W^{s}(\mathbf{q}), which indicates that these solutions are robust under small changes of parameter values.

A relevant fact regarding the homoclinic orbit Γq\Gamma_{q} is that it presents Shilnikov focus-focus homoclinic chaos in a concrete model vector field. Indeed, most of the studies about this bifurcation have been carried out (so far) only theoretically [19, 52]. Moreover, as far as we know, this work represents the first example of the actual computation of a global two-dimensional invariant manifold involved in a focus-focus homoclinic bifurcation in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}.

We also performed a thorough search for traveling waves connecting stationary states with V=0V=0 to invariant objects with U,V>0U,V>0 in each parameter region in Fig. 4 (In the particular case of pmp_{m}, we chose c=10c=10 in order to ensure its eigenvalues are real). This procedure involved the computation of 3D and 4D unstable manifolds of equilibria p1p_{1} and pmp_{m}, respectively, following the scheme from [11]. Unfortunately, all the computed orbits have negative (U,V)(U,V) coordinates for some z>0z>0 and, hence, did not match our initial criterium of non-negativity.

While the amplitude of the solutions we found may be rather small, it is important to emphasize that our results are qualitative; that is, our aim was not to present specifically quantitative features of the predator-prey interaction on which the system is based, but to show what kind of dynamical behavior one may hope to find, either theoretically or numerically. That said, the amplitude of the oscillations varies in markedly different scales for the rescaled variables, and variations in VV are much more pronounced than those of UU for pulses, fronts and trains. This difference in amplitudes can be explained by paying attention to the following observations: (i) quantities uu and vv spatially spread at distinct rates. This rate difference provides that the low-diffusivity variable promotes a heterogeneous aggregation of both variables along the domain; in consequence, both traveling-wave profiles propagate in a spatially non-homogenous shape, regardless of d<1d<1 or d>1d>1; (ii) the ratio in the original variables u/vu/v prevails as both amplitudes are of the same order in any scenarios here considered; (iii) upon integrating system (2) along finite spatial domain, and assuming uniform convergence in time, we obtain that solutions satisfy formulae:

(18a) ∫−LL[s​u​(u−m)​(1−u)​(u+v)−a​u​v]​d​x=d​ℬ1d​t,\displaystyle\displaystyle\int\limits_{-L}^{L}\left[su(u-m)(1-u)(u+v)-auv\right]\>\text{d}x=\dfrac{d\mathcal{B}_{1}}{dt}\,,
(18b) ∫−LL[b​u​v−g​v​(u+v)]​d​x=d​ℬ2d​t,\displaystyle\displaystyle\int\limits_{-L}^{L}\left[buv-gv(u+v)\right]\>\text{d}x=\dfrac{d\mathcal{B}_{2}}{dt}\,,

where the total “masses” are given by ℬ1​(t)=∫−LLu​d​x\mathcal{B}_{1}(t)=\int_{-L}^{L}u\>\text{d}x and ℬ2​(t)=∫−LLv​d​x\mathcal{B}_{2}(t)=\int_{-L}^{L}v\>\text{d}x, regardless of whether the boundary conditions for uxu_{x} and vxv_{x} vanish or cancel out each other at x=±Lx=\pm L. Moreover, once we define the weighted total mass by ℬ⁡(t):=b​ℬ1​(t)+a​ℬ2​(t)\mathcal{B}(t):=b\mathcal{B}_{1}(t)+a\mathcal{B}_{2}(t), from (18), we obtain formula

(19) ∫−LL[b​s​u​(u−m)​(1−u)−a​g​v]​(u+v)​d​x=d​ℬd​t.\displaystyle\int\limits_{-L}^{L}\left[bsu(u-m)(1-u)-agv\right](u+v)\>\text{d}x=\dfrac{d\mathcal{B}}{dt}\,.

Upon taking into account L≫1L\gg 1, we get traveling-wave solutions of (2), which are characterized by having profiles that keep their shape over time. Now, we consider a moving interval-frame 𝒥=[−L−c​t,L−c​t]\mathcal{J}=[-L-ct,L-ct], which “runs alongside” the traveling profiles with the same speed c≥0c\geq 0. In so doing, integral in the left-hand side term of (19) over 𝒥\mathcal{J} is constant for all t≥0t\geq 0. That is, since traveling-wave profiles displacement only changes their position in time, the weighted total mass traveling speed is therefore conserved, i.e. d​ℬ/d​t≡𝒞0d\mathcal{B}/dt\equiv\mathcal{C}_{0}, where 𝒞0\mathcal{C}_{0} is constant. Thus, as u+v≥0u+v\geq 0 for all |x|≤L|x|\leq L, the total masses of the two variables follow a conservation-like property for traveling-wave solutions. Namely, as the wave variable z=x+c​tz=x+ct corresponds to a spatial translation for t≥0t\geq 0, variable amplitudes balance each other to satisfy identity (19) for a constant weighted total mass rate of change 𝒞0\mathcal{C}_{0}.

It is interesting to note that identities in (18) are also satisfied for stationary solutions; that is, upon setting ut=vt=0u_{t}=v_{t}=0, we have relation (19) with d​ℬ/d​t≡0d\mathcal{B}/dt\equiv 0, when homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions are in place. Similar identities are obtained for Dirichlet, periodic and mixed-type boundary conditions, as well. In addition, this model may be able to develop diffusion-driven instabilities by means of Turing bifurcations. Nonetheless, in order to perform such an analysis, a stationary spatial pattern setting must be taken into account.

Finally, we studied the stability of every wave solution we detected, and we found that each of them is unstable. We followed the approach from [8, 44, 45]: In a general PDE of the form

𝐮t\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{t} =𝐟⁡(𝐮)+D​𝐮x​x,\displaystyle=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})+D\,\mathbf{u}_{xx},

traveling waves are functions 𝐔⁡(z)\mathbf{U}(z), where z=x+c​tz=x+ct. In particular, defining the new pair of variables (ξ,t)=(x+c​t,t)(\xi,t)=(x+ct,t), we have that

𝐮t=c​𝐮ξ+𝐮t,𝐮x​x=𝐮ξ​ξ.\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{t}=c\,\mathbf{u}_{\xi}+\mathbf{u}_{t},\qquad\mathbf{u}_{xx}=\mathbf{u}_{\xi\xi}.

This implies that the system can be written as

(20) 𝐮t=−c​𝐮ξ+𝐟⁡(𝐮)+D​𝐮ξ​ξ.\mathbf{u}_{t}=-c\,\mathbf{u}_{\xi}+\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})+D\,\mathbf{u}_{\xi\xi}.

In our case, 𝐮=(u,v)\mathbf{u}=(u,v), 𝐟\mathbf{f} stands for the reaction part of (2), and D=(d001).D=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}d&0\\ 0&1\end{array}\right). Notice that when 𝐮t=𝟎\mathbf{u}_{t}=\mathbf{0} in (20) we recover the ODE system (2) for traveling waves. This means that traveling waves are a stationary solution of (20). We then linearized it and evaluated the traveling waves we found. In particular, we obtained the spectral stability by numerically computing the ten eigenvalues with the largest real part of the Jacobian matrix of (20) and noticed that (in every run) the spectrum obtained had at least one eigenvalue with positive real part. We also tried with different mesh refinements and the results were consistent.

Last but not least, as a consequence of recasting a reaction-diffusion equation as a dynamical system with infinite dimensions, the multiplicity of solutions is large —one for each initial condition. As the solutions we found turned out to be unstable, we focused on highlighting the zoo of travelling waves of the system stressing the analysis of the chaotic behavior of such solutions. Hence, no integration of the reaction-diffusion system was carried out since that would not help to clarify the ideas about the analysis here presented. Disregarding the fact that the solutions are unstable, the analysis performed here is novel in the area of dynamical systems and we expect this to provide future guidance to study Shilnikov homoclinic focus-focus chaos with an emphasis on the stable and unstable manifolds of related homogeneous steady states.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
